entities.name: Baysonqor
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ghiyath ud-din Baysunghur (1397–1433), known primarily as Baysonqor, was a pivotal figure in the cultural efflorescence of the Timurid Empire, serving as a prince, military commander, and, most enduringly, as the preeminent patron of arts during his era. A grandson of the formidable conqueror Timur and son of Shah Rukh, Baysonqor operated from the intellectual and artistic hub of Herat, transforming it into a beacon of Persianate culture. His brief but impactful life established him as the leading patron of the Persian miniature, a master calligrapher, and a driving force behind the systematic preservation and production of illuminated manuscripts that defined the Timurid Renaissance.

Baysonqor's direct contributions to the arts were manifold, most notably through his establishment of the royal atelier (kitabkhana) in Herat, which employed dozens of calligraphers, painters, gilders, and binders. This workshop produced some of the most exquisite examples of Islamic art, including the monumental Baysunghur Shahnameh, completed around 1430, a lavishly illustrated manuscript containing over 30,000 couplets of Ferdowsi's epic poem. Beyond this magnum opus, Baysonqor personally supervised the creation of numerous other calligraphic and illustrated works, demonstrating his profound understanding and appreciation for artistic craftsmanship. His own skill as a calligrapher, particularly in the thuluth and naskh scripts, further solidified his reputation as an artist-prince.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Baysonqor's patronage fundamentally shaped Persian and Islamic art, producing masterpieces like the Baysunghur Shahnameh and establishing an atelier model that influenced future dynasties across the Middle East and India. His efforts ensured the transmission of a distinct artistic style for centuries.
